scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The theoretical foundations of Gaudiya Nritya derive from the ancient Sanskrit treatise Natyashastra.

Physical evidence of its historic practice is visible in temple sculptures and archaeological sites across Bengal associated with Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, as well as in ancient Bengali poetry.
Historical literature attests to the style; notably, the 17th-century Sanskrit treatise Abhinaya Chandrika by Maheswara Mohapatra of Odisha lists Gaudiya dance as one of seven regional dance styles.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Gaudiya Nritya is a devotional classical art form traditionally executed to express religious narratives and philosophical concepts.
Its performances convey Vaishnavite devotional themes, Shakta religious ideas, and veneration of deities such as Shiva and Ganesha through songs composed by ancient poets.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music in Gaudiya Nritya is centered on sacred Hindu traditions, primarily Vaishnavism, Shakta themes, and songs dedicated to Shiva and Ganesha.
Kirtana forms the musical mainstay, classified as a Medini type of Prabandha-giti featuring six angas (svara, viruda, pada, tenaka, pata, tala).
The pulse is Variable multi-meter cycles determined by varṇakāla (4 to 68 units).

The soundscape of Gaudiya Nritya is characterized by resonant, complex drumming from the Pakhavaj and Shrikhol supporting classical devotional singing. Verses follow classical ragas and structured Prabandha-giti forms like Kirtana, built over precise rhythmic metric cycles.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical and contemporary figures associated with Gaudiya Nritya include researcher Mahua Mukherjee, who reconstructed the form in the 1980s; Indologist Bratindra Nath Mukhopadhyay, who advised adopting its formal name in 1994; and 17th-century musicologist Sangeet Shastrakar Maheswara Mohapatra, who documented the style in his treatise Abhinaya Chandrika.

Rooted in the ancient temple traditions of Gauda (Bengal) during the Pala and Sena periods, the lineage of Gaudiya Nritya traces back through Natyashastra theory and medieval treatises like Abhinaya Chandrika.
